The nineteen-sixty-two Seattle World's Fair, officially titled Century Twenty-one Exposition, celebrated humanity's optimism about space exploration and the future as the Space Race intensified. The fair was themed "Century Twenty-one" to emphasise the promise of space-age technology and to capture the excitement of the Space Race, which coincided directly with American efforts to reach the moon. Anchored by the iconic Space Needle, a striking six-hundred-five-foot observation tower designed by architect John Graham Junior, the fair attracted nearly ten million visitors from across the continent. The Space Needle has become an enduring symbol of Seattle and remains one of the most recognisable structures representing the era's optimistic futurism. The tower continues to dominate Seattle's skyline to this day. The fair included a working Monorail system that connected various fair attractions, representing the advanced urban transportation and automation ideals that the era championed. Visitors could experience this futuristic transit firsthand. The exposition displayed exhibits focused on science, technology, and space exploration, reflecting the period's fascination with the cosmos and scientific advancement. Rockets, satellites, and space hardware captured visitors' imagination. The fair was held on seventy-four acres in Seattle Center, which was subsequently developed into a permanent cultural district hosting museums, theatres, and public spaces that remain active venues today. The fair established the template for post-war world's fairs that emphasised science, technology, and forward-looking cultural narratives about humanity's future.
